title: Acid-Base Chemistry
seo_title: Secondary 3 Chemistry: Acid-Base Chemistry Worksheets (O-Level 6092 with Answers)
standard_text: Describe acids in terms of hydrogen ions and alkalis in terms of hydroxide ions; describe the pH scale and the use of Universal Indicator; distinguish between strong and weak acids and alkalis; describe neutralisation as H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O and the reactions of acids with metals, bases and carbonates; describe the preparation, separation and purification of salts using the solubility rules; describe the manufacture of ammonia by the Haber process and the idea of a reversible reaction; classify oxides as acidic, basic, amphoteric or neutral (summary of the Singapore-Cambridge O-Level Chemistry 6092 syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 3 O-Level Chemistry worksheets on acid-base chemistry: acids and alkalis, pH and indicators, strong and weak acids, neutralisation, preparing salts, solubility rules, the Haber process and types of oxides. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Acids give H⁺; alkalis give OH⁻.
key_sub: Choose the salt method from the solubility rules.
body_html:
How to think about it

Acids produce H⁺ ions in water; alkalis produce OH⁻ ions.

  • pH below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 alkaline. Strong acids and alkalis ionise completely.
  • acid + metal → salt + hydrogen; acid + base → salt + water; acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide.
  • Salts: titration (Na, K, ammonium salts), excess insoluble solid then filter (other soluble salts), precipitation (insoluble salts).
  • Oxides: non-metal oxides acidic, metal oxides basic, Al₂O₃ and ZnO amphoteric, CO and NO neutral. Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, 450 °C, 200 atm, iron catalyst.
Example

How do you make zinc sulfate crystals?

add excess zinc oxide to dilute sulfuric acid

filter

heat to saturation and cool

Answer: crystallisation

Example

How do you make lead(II) chloride?

it is insoluble

mix lead(II) nitrate and sodium chloride solutions

filter, wash, dry

Answer: precipitation

Common mistakes

  • Using 'weak' to mean 'dilute'.
  • Making every salt by titration.
  • Thinking lead(II) chloride and silver chloride are soluble.
  • Thinking all metal oxides are only basic: Al₂O₃ and ZnO are amphoteric.

faq.q: How do you choose a method to make a salt?
faq.a: If the salt is insoluble, use precipitation. If it is a soluble sodium, potassium or ammonium salt, use titration. For other soluble salts, add an excess of the insoluble metal, base or carbonate to the acid and filter.

faq.q: What is the difference between a strong acid and a weak acid?
faq.a: A strong acid ionises completely in water to give H⁺ ions; a weak acid ionises only partially, so it has fewer H⁺ ions at the same concentration.

faq.q: What conditions are used in the Haber process?
faq.a: About 450 °C, a pressure of about 200 atmospheres and an iron catalyst, with unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen recycled.
